answer.policy_title: Total Ankle Arthroplasty – Medical Clinical Policy Bulletin
answer.effective_date: The Aetna policy page does not display an effective or last-revised date in the retrieved content. An independently indexed Aetna-policy reference reports a last review date of 2025-03-12, but that date could not be verified on Aetna's policy page.
criteria_quotes: Aetna considers total ankle arthroplasty (TAA) using a Food and Drug Administration-cleared implant medically necessary when the following criteria are met:

TAA is used to replace an arthritic or severely degenerated ankle; and Member is skeletally mature; and Member has moderate or severe pain with loss of ankle mobility and function; and Imaging is consistent with severe arthritis / degeneration of the ankle due to osteoarthritis (degenerative arthritis), post-traumatic arthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, or inflammatory arthritis; and Member has failed at least 6 months of conservative management (including physical therapy by a licensed physical therapist, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and orthoses as indicated); and If member is diabetic, their hemoglobin A1C (HbA1c) should be less than 8 percent within 3 months prior to surgery; and Member has none of the contraindications to TAA listed below.

The policy's physical-therapy footnote states that physical therapy must be in-person, recent (within the past year), for at least 6 weeks—or 12 weeks if the member is younger than 50 or has a BMI greater than 40—and confirmed by actual PT notes or claims-history documentation. Conservative therapy may be inappropriate and not required for severe osteoarthritis with bone-on-bone articulation in the weight-bearing portion of the joint.

The listed contraindications include: absence of the medial or lateral malleolus; active or prior deep infection in the ankle joint or adjacent bones; avascular necrosis of the talus; Charcot joint; corticosteroid injection into the joint within 12 weeks of planned arthroplasty; hindfoot or forefoot malalignment precluding a plantigrade foot; insufficient bone or musculature for proper component positioning or alignment; insufficient ligament support that cannot be repaired with soft-tissue stabilization; lower-extremity vascular insufficiency; neuromuscular disease causing lack of normal muscle function about the affected ankle; osteonecrosis; peripheral neuropathy; poor skin or soft-tissue quality; prior ankle arthrodesis; prior surgery or injury adversely affecting ankle-bone quality; psychiatric problems hindering adequate perioperative cooperation; severe adjacent-structure deformity; severe ankle deformity not normally eligible for arthroplasty; severe osteoporosis, osteopenia, or other poor bone quality; significant knee malalignment; skeletal immaturity; and vascular insufficiency in the affected limb.
The policy states that revision TAA is medically necessary for individuals with a failed total ankle prosthesis and that TAA is experimental, investigational, or unproven for other indications.
answer.appeal_deadline: 2027-02-16. The denial notice states that the appeal must be received within 180 days of 2026-08-20.
answer.submission_route: Submit a written pre-service member appeal using the address or instructions on the denial notice. Aetna's Member Complaint and Appeal Form also permits submission by mail to Aetna, P.O. Box 14463, Lexington, KY 40512, or by fax to 859-425-3379. The form says the member may instead call the Member Services number on the Aetna ID card. Include Cameron Carter's member ID, the denial reference number POC-C3B0DB0F14-18449, CPT 27702, the requested total ankle replacement, the denial notice, a clear explanation of disagreement, and supporting medical records. The provider may also submit supporting documentation through Availity or Aetna's provider appeal process.
answer.how_to_obtain_criteria: Ask Aetna Member Services using the number on the ID card, and ask specifically for: (1) the complete clinical policy and clinical review criteria applied to reference POC-C3B0DB0F14-18449; (2) the specific criterion or criteria that Aetna found unmet; (3) the clinical rationale and records relied upon; and (4) the applicable plan certificate or evidence of coverage. The public policy states that the member's benefit plan governs if it conflicts with an Aetna Clinical Policy Bulletin. Ask the treating provider to request the case-specific utilization-review rationale and peer-review information as part of the appeal.
answer.notes: Aetna's publicly available Clinical Policy Bulletin 0645 expressly lists CPT 27702, 'Arthroplasty, ankle; with implant (total ankle),' as covered when the selection criteria are met. The notice does not identify which particular criterion was considered unmet, so the denial cannot be matched to a specific failure without the case-specific review rationale. The publicly retrieved Aetna page did not expose an effective or revision date; the 2025-03-12 last-review date comes from an independently indexed reference and should be confirmed with Aetna.

Medical Necessity Aetna considers total ankle arthroplasty (TAA) using a Food and Drug Administration-cleared implant (e.g., the Agility LP Total Ankle, the Eclipse Total Ankle, the INBONE Total Ankle, the Infinity Total Ankle System, the STAR system, the Salto Talaris Total Ankle Prosthesis, and the Zimmer Trabecular Metal Total Ankle) medically necessary when the following criteria are met: TAA is used to replace an arthritic or severely degenerated ankle; and Member is skeletally mature; and Member has with moderate or severe pain with loss of ankle mobility and function; and Imaging is consistent with severe arthritis / degeneration of the ankle due to osteoarthritis (degenerative arthritis), post-traumatic arthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, or inflammatory arthritis; and Member has have failed at least 6 months of conservative management (including physical therapy Footnote1 * by a licensed physical therapist, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and orthoses as indicated); and If member is diabetic, their hemoglobin A1C (HbA1c) should be less than 8 percent within 3 months prior to surgery; and Member has none of the contraindications to TAA listed below: Absence of the medial or lateral malleolus Active or prior deep infection in the ankle joint or adjacent bones Avascular necrosis of the talus Charcot joint Corticosteroid injection into the joint within 12 weeks of the planned arthroplasty Hindfoot or forefoot mal-alignment precluding plantigrade foot Insufficient bone or musculature such that proper component positioning or alignment is not possible Insufficient ligament support that can not be repaired with soft tissue stabilization Lower extremity vascular insufficiency Neuromuscular disease resulting in lack of normal muscle function about the affected ankle Osteonecrosis Peripheral neuropathy (may lead to Charcot joint of the affected ankle) Poor skin and soft tissue quality about the surgical site Prior arthrodesis (fusion) at the ankle joint Prior surgery or injury that has adversely affected ankle bone quality Psychiatric problems that hinder adequate cooperation during peri-operative period Severe anatomic deformity in adjacent ankle structures, including hindfoot, forefoot and knee joint Severe ankle deformity (e.g., severe varus or valgus deformity) that would not normally be eligible for ankle arthroplasty Severe osteoporosis, osteopenia or other conditions resulting in poor bone quality, as this may result in inadequate bony fixation Significant mal-alignment of the knee joint Skeletal maturity not yet reached Vascular insufficiency in the affected limb. Conservative therapy may be inappropriate and not required for severe osteoarthritis with bone-on-bone articulation in the weight-bearing portion of the joint. Aetna considers revision TAA medically necessary for individuals with failed total ankle prosthesis. Aetna considers TAA experimental, investigational, or unproven for all other indications because its effectiveness for indications other than the ones listed above has not been established. Any health care professional (licensed individual or groups) that provides health services to our members can dispute a decision. We do not charge for disputes. What's the difference between a reconsideration and an appeal? We offer two ways to dispute a claim decision: with a reconsideration or an appeal. We don't charge for either. What's a reconsideration? A reconsideration is a formal review of a previous claim decision. It covers reimbursement decisions, coding decisions and claims that need to be reprocessed. Some claims skip reconsideration and go straight to appeal. These include: Adverse initial claim decisions based on medical necessity, a payment policy, or experimental/investigational coverage Denials for non-inpatient hospital services with no precertification Adverse initial utilization review decisions Retroactive authorizations Medicare nonparticipating review decisions Some non-Medicare claims under state legislation Submitted a reconsideration that should be an appeal? We'll route it to the right place. What's an appeal? An appeal is a written request to change or overturn a previous decision. That includes reconsideration decisions and initial utilization review or clinical claim decisions. Appeals apply when a decision was based on: Medical necessity A payment policy Experimental or investigational coverage criteria Some situations go directly to appeal. They skip reconsideration entirely. These include: Adverse initial inpatient claim decisions Outpatient service denials for no precertification Adverse utilization review decisions Retroactive authorizations How the reconsideration process works You need to file your reconsideration within 180 calendar days of the initial claim decision.     "TAA is used to replace an arthritic or severely degenerated ankle; and Member is skeletally mature; and Member has moderate or severe pain with loss of ankle mobility and function; and Imaging is consistent with severe arthritis / degeneration of the ankle due to osteoarthritis (degenerative arthritis), post-traumatic arthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, or inflammatory arthritis; and Member has failed at least 6 months of conservative management (including physical therapy by a licensed physical therapist, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and orthoses as indicated); and If member is diabetic, their hemoglobin A1C (HbA1c) should be less than 8 percent within 3 months prior to surgery; and Member has none of the contraindications to TAA listed below.",

    "The listed contraindications include: absence of the medial or lateral malleolus; active or prior deep infection in the ankle joint or adjacent bones; avascular necrosis of the talus; Charcot joint; corticosteroid injection into the joint within 12 weeks of planned arthroplasty; hindfoot or forefoot malalignment precluding a plantigrade foot; insufficient bone or musculature for proper component positioning or alignment; insufficient ligament support that cannot be repaired with soft-tissue stabilization; lower-extremity vascular insufficiency; neuromuscular disease causing lack of normal muscle function about the affected ankle; osteonecrosis; peripheral neuropathy; poor skin or soft-tissue quality; prior ankle arthrodesis; prior surgery or injury adversely affecting ankle-bone quality; psychiatric problems hindering adequate perioperative cooperation; severe adjacent-structure deformity; severe ankle deformity not normally eligible for arthroplasty; severe osteoporosis, osteopenia, or other poor bone quality; significant knee malalignment; skeletal immaturity; and vascular insufficiency in the affected limb.",
